wa_mount_baker_park_glacier_headwall.notes: Access ramp across the bergschrund; narrow ledge traverse and step-chopping may be needed at the lip.
Sustained ice pitches to the ridge crest.
An overhanging cornice lip near the ridge crest/summit plateau has been noted in historical accounts (~8 ft).

wa_mount_stuart_stuart_glacier_couloir.notes: Start at about 7,800 ft at the top of the Stuart Glacier. The bergschrund below the couloir can be the first real obstacle: in sugary spring snow a safe crossing is hard to find, so be ready to belay it. Above, the gully runs at 40–50° and narrows steadily for a few hundred feet toward the first step.

The crux sits in the narrowest part of the couloir, roughly halfway up: a short steep step that often holds around 100 ft of water ice up to 60°, with sections described as near 80°. It can be anything from firm snow to verglas over rock, so bring screws and a few rock pieces and expect to pitch it out in lean conditions.
A little above the first step a second, shorter step of rock or ice interrupts the gully. It is brief, but thin ice over rock here protects poorly; above it the couloir widens out.

The couloir opens into a wider snowfield. Climb a couple hundred feet of sustained 50° snow to the small notch on the upper West Ridge. Late in the day this slope softens and becomes tiring; the exit rocks at the notch are low 5th class on the normal finish, or about 5.7 on the left-hand variation.

From the notch, drop about 10 ft onto the south side and follow ledges along the south flank of the ridge. In early season these ledges are commonly rimed and iced, and the traversing and short downclimbs are harder to protect than the grade suggests.
Easy fifth-class ground that steepens toward the top of the pitch. Stay on the south side rather than being drawn onto the colder, more exposed north face.
Traverse diagonally across mid-fifth-class rock into a gully that leads back up to the crest. With rime on the rock this is mixed climbing in crampons, often graded M3–M5 depending on season.

Class 3 ledges link short crack systems of mid-fifth-class climbing to the summit block. Near the top a short 5.6 lieback can be bypassed by a delicate traverse across the upper north face; the final moves to the summit follow a down-sloping ledge that holds ice early in the year and takes little protection.

wa_dragontail_peak_r4.notes: From Colchuck Lake, aim for the lowest rock protrusion near the middle of the face and bear slightly left. There are two possible starts (left or right) into the first couloir, which cannot be seen from the lake. Climb about 800 ft of 40–50° snow, sometimes with a tongue of blue ice to the right that takes screws. Most parties simul-climb or solo this section.

About three pitches of 70–80° ice gullies over slabby rock link the first and second couloirs, rated up to M3 when lean. Some years it is fat, easy ice; other years a paper-thin sheet protected by pins and rock gear more than screws. There are two alternatives: a left-trending steep snow ramp, followed by a 20 m rappel from a fixed anchor, or a 5.8 rock bypass.
Over 600 ft of 40–50° snow and ice. Some seasons it holds a short AI3 step. After a dry spell it can be knee-deep unconsolidated snow that is slow and exhausting; parties typically simul-climb it.

A short steep band separates the second and third couloirs. Exit up and right, either by a mixed pitch or a steep snow pitch depending on conditions. The band ranges from thick easy ice to runout, thin mixed climbing on slab that is hard to protect, so plan to belay it.

A few hundred feet of snow at a similar or slightly lower angle cuts behind the Fin, the prominent rock feature on the upper face. It sometimes holds a short, thick WI2 step and ends on an open slope a couple hundred feet below the summit.
A short snow scramble and traversing slope from the top of the third couloir reach the summit. Descend by the long traverse to Asgard Pass.

wa_eldorado_peak_northeast_face.notes: Around 7,500 ft, leave the standard East Ridge track and traverse climber's right onto the Northeast Face, staying above the steep cliffs that guard its lower edge. This is crevassed glacier ground, so stay roped with crevasse rescue gear.

Traverse the face below the rock band. Late in summer there are two levels: a low line below a significant crevasse at about 8,100 ft, and a higher line above that crevasse but below the bergschrund and rock band at about 8,400 ft. The usual track runs under the band near 8,200 ft, paralleling the big crevasse, to a point roughly northeast of the summit.

Turn uphill and climb the face, several pitches up to 60°, to the base of the summit knife-edge; a running belay on pickets and ice screws is the usual protection. A direct line above the bergschrund can hold ice to about AI2+, and a harder variation crosses the schrund and climbs a snowy ramp through the rock band to an exposed 60° ice slope. Snow or bare ice depends on recent weather.

Rejoin the East Ridge at the start of the knife-edge, around 8,700 ft, and follow the exposed crest to the summit. Hard ice just below the edge can take screws, while pickets may need heavy driving. East Ridge parties share this crest, so expect traffic and plan belays that do not block it.

wa_mount_rainier_mowich_face.notes: From the glacier camps below the face (about 9,600-10,200 ft, near the divide with the Edmunds Glacier), stay roped and climb the last of the North Mowich Glacier to the foot of the face. Watch for fresh rockfall debris on the ice: it marks the fall lines coming off the face. Start in the dark so the face is climbed before sun hits it.

The bergschrund under the central face is large and can be impassable late season. It is usually bypassed through a rock band on the climber's left; earlier in the year a snow bridge may go after weaving around the biggest crevasses. Belay the crossing if the bridge is thin.

The lower two-thirds of the face runs at roughly 35–42° on solid snow in good conditions, climbed with running protection on pickets. Near 12,000 ft the surface turns to harder ice and demands more careful technique. The whole face is exposed to rockfall and ice shards; climbing before the sun arrives reduces but does not remove the hazard.

Around 12,500 ft the line splits. The original (Grade III) cuts left into an hourglass of snow, ice and rock, gains a snow ledge around the rock, then a 40–50° ramp. The harder (Grade IV) variation cuts right over one or two AI2–3 ice steps and 4–6 pitches of 50–60° snow. Wrong gullies here dead-end in cliffs; carry screws.

The face tops out on a bench near 13,300 ft; high up a windlip or choke often needs a short traverse on firmer snow. From the bench, slushy sun cups or penitentes lead to Liberty Cap (14,112 ft). The descent is a carryover down the Emmons-Winthrop or Disappointment Cleaver, not the face.

wa_mount_shuksan_price_glacier.notes: From the slab bivy, gain the ridge crest and the glacier margin, traverse right to the exposed snow saddle below Nooksack Tower, then drop and work onto the main lobe near 6,500 ft; the gully under the tower is a rock- and icefall path, so cross it fast. Above, weave up steep snow and alpine ice (AI2-AI3) between seracs and slough chutes. Late season means bare ice and climbing into and out of the overhanging walls of crevasses.

The bergschrund band near 7,800 ft, which may be one crack or several. There are three ways over: rock on the left, an ice line in the middle, or mixed ground on the right. Which one goes changes with the season, from an AI3 ice rib to an AI4 ice chimney late in the year; in a big-snow year the left edge can be filled in. Carry screws, pickets and a small rock rack.

Above the schrund, climb the steep snow or ice field to the glacier plateau below the summit pyramid, then cross the plateau and swing around to the pyramid's south side. Crevasses remain on the plateau, and the snow here softens early on a warm day.

Finish up the easy gullies on the south side of the summit pyramid (4th to low 5th class), the same central gully the Sulphide route uses, with a few rock moves low and again near the top. Expect other parties and rockfall; the descent reverses this gully toward Hell's Highway.

wa_colchuck_peak_holsten_hilden.notes: Start right of the Northeast Couloir, at the foot of the Hidden Couloir. Two rope-stretching pitches of ice lead into the couloir. They take screws well when formed, and grades given range from AI3 to AI3+. This is the most reliable ice on the route; the ground above depends on winter snow conditions.

Start right of the Northeast Couloir, at the foot of the Hidden Couloir. Two rope-stretching pitches of ice lead into the couloir. They take screws well when formed, and grades given range from AI3 to AI3+. This is the most reliable ice on the route; the ground above depends on winter snow conditions.
Leave the Hidden Couloir and climb a few hundred feet of 50–60° snow up and left toward a steep rock band. Protection is sparse, so carry a picket, and the slope loads with wind-drifted snow.

Two pitches of unconsolidated snow over moderate rock. Clear the snow to find placements for rock gear and pins, and move carefully: the snow gives little hold for tools, and a slip here runs down the slope below.
Traverse about 30 ft left into a chimney and climb two pitches of M6 mixed ground up it. Stubby screws, pitons and small cams protect it. This is the sustained technical heart of the route.
More steep snow leads to a final rock band. Climb through it to a notch on the north ridge crest.
Out of the north-ridge notch, a tricky wide crack at M6 is the last hard move. From its top, traverse around to the west into the final couloir of the North Buttress Couloir route.
Up the final couloir of the North Buttress Couloir line, one more short but steep mixed pitch reaches the summit, which is often rimed and windswept in winter. Descend by the Colchuck Glacier.

wa_lincoln_peak_standard.notes: From the SW buttress base, ascend snow slopes toward the first bergschrund.
Cross a snow bridge and climb directly up the face of a ~50-ft serac.
Two roped 60m pitches through narrow gullies with runnel crossings.
Knife-edge arete requiring careful tool and crampon placement.
Final ~20 ft of scrambling on loose rock past crumbling rime-ice features to the summit.

wa_mount_logan_fremont_glacier.grade: Hiking, mix of forest and meadow terrain
wa_mount_logan_fremont_glacier.notes: Multiple creek crossings, persistent snow late June/early July crosses the trail, ice axe recommended early season for icy sections
wa_mount_logan_fremont_glacier.pitch: 1-2: Approach via Thunder Creek Trail to Park Creek Pass

wa_mount_logan_fremont_glacier.notes: Gently rising traverse across high alpine, crosses rib at 7,600 ft, steep gully passage through cliff bands around 7,350 ft with possible snow/ice
Gentle glacier traverse, roped team recommended, crevasses generally small and avoidable but present
Steeper glacier leading to south ridge (Hogsback), moat crossing to access ridge crest, late-season snow bridge may be absent

Approximately 300 vertical feet of scrambling, cross Hogsback notch, descend briefly then traverse ledges on east side of summit ridge, final 100 feet Class 3-4 with good holds and solid rock, some exposure
wa_mount_logan_fremont_glacier.pitch: 6: Summit scramble via Hogsback and east side

wa_mount_rainier_liberty_ridge.notes: Drop off Curtis Ridge onto the Carbon Glacier at about 7,300 ft and cross to the toe of the ridge near 8,600 ft. In May and June several lines usually go; later the glacier breaks up. The usual crux is the moat between glacier and ridge, which has turned strong parties back. The ridge can be gained from either flank or directly at the toe.

The crest proper from the toe has loose rocky steps and uneven climbing; a flank gives steadier snow but sits under rockfall. The east flank is steeper with more rock bands, so parties starting there cross over the crest to the west side and continue to Thumb Rock, the obvious gendarme near 10,500 ft. Rocks come down without warning here, so climb it early in the day.

The small saddle just above Thumb Rock is the only real bivouac on the ridge, limited to twelve people. Dig platforms and build a wall against wind and the small rocks that fall from the cliff above. Above this point no safe bivy exists, and retreat grows harder than continuing up, so settle the weather forecast and team condition here.

Above camp a rock band (the Gun Sight) blocks the crest. The easiest line goes out left (east) around it and up the east side of the ridge; when it is formed, a short water-ice pitch goes straight through the middle. The right-hand bypass crosses under loose rock and is the poorest choice. Rockfall off the Gun Sight has triggered a very large slab avalanche on the slope below.

Climb up and left to pass the Black Pyramid, a dark rock buttress over 1,000 ft tall, on its left (east) side from about 11,800 to 12,800 ft. The ground is steep snow or low-angle alpine ice depending on the season, on exposed faces reported up to 60°. Screws and pickets for running protection; regain the rounded crest above the Pyramid at 12,800 ft.

The bergschrund near 13,800 ft is the last and usually hardest obstacle. In some years it is a step over a small crack and a snow ramp; in others an offset gap with a thin, awkward bridge and a near-vertical wall above. Anchor the belayer and pitch it out when it is dicey, and belay out of the fall line, since sun-baked or wind-hammered ice here breaks off in large plates.

Above the schrund, slopes ease to Liberty Cap at about 14,110 ft; fast or grinding depending on the surface. Columbia Crest is over a mile away: most parties drop about 600 ft to Liberty Saddle to join the Emmons-Winthrop descent, and the Crest adds about 800 ft of climbing from the saddle. Stay roped through the saddle, where crevasses are thinly bridged and cornices form on its east side.

wa_mount_rainier_ptarmigan_ridge.notes: From the high camp at about 10,200–10,300 ft below the Ptarmigan ice cliffs, descend onto the Mowich Glacier to the bergschrund at about 9,800 ft, crossing avalanche-prone slopes on the way. The usual crossing is a snow bridge just left of a rock outcrop near the middle of the face.

Above the schrund make a rising traverse back east toward the ice cliffs, threading an obvious passage through the rock bands on about 1,000 ft of 40–45° snow. Staying close under the cliffs on the right keeps the route-finding simple as far as the hourglass. Lower-face snow can be rotten and unsupportive once it warms.

At a steep rock band traverse left into the hourglass-shaped snow face and climb it on either side to the base of the big rock buttress that splits the upper route (~11,500 ft). Exposed; protect with pickets and screws, and belay if rockfall is active. At the buttress the 1935 line goes left and contours onto the slopes between the buttress and the icefall (45–55°, often icy); most parties now go right.

From the toe of the buttress climb a short way to the final ice slope, typically several hundred feet of blue ice around 55°, then cross a rock rib and traverse snow or ice to the exit chute, the first major break in the ridge's cliffs. The chute is easy 5th class with a near-vertical step that may hold a fixed pin or two; rock is fractured, so bring screws plus a light rock rack and pins.
wa_mount_rainier_ptarmigan_ridge.pitch: Right variation: ice slope and exit chute

wa_mount_rainier_ptarmigan_ridge.notes: Above the chute, easier scrambling leads onto the Liberty Cap Glacier. Climb about 1,000 ft of glacier slopes, cut back right to the ridge crest through the crevasse pattern, and follow easy slopes along the crest to Liberty Cap (~14,110 ft). Good bivy sites exist on the lower Liberty Cap Glacier. Surface conditions decide whether this is quick or a grind.
wa_mount_rainier_ptarmigan_ridge.pitch: Liberty Cap Glacier to Liberty Cap

wa_mount_rainier_ptarmigan_ridge.notes: Columbia Crest is more than a mile away: drop about 600 ft into Liberty Saddle and climb about 800 ft back up to the summit. Stay roped, since crevasses between Liberty Cap and the crest can be thinly bridged and deep, and large cornices form on the east side of the saddle. The descent via the Emmons–Winthrop leaves from the saddle.

wa_sw_couloir_and_face.notes: Start from the upper SE corner of the Lower Curtis Glacier, on the snow slope below the obvious glacier tongue that reaches halfway up the face, aiming for the narrow gully at the right side of the main wall. The slope steepens to about 45° near its top and ends at a large transverse crevasse, crossed on a snow bridge; check the bridge before committing.

Above the crevasse a short band of vertical ice forms in an open-book rock corner, climbed as an ice-filled chimney in its middle, followed immediately by a second, shorter vertical step. This is the steepest ice on the route; carry a tool as well as an axe and a couple of screws.
Steep snow continues above the ice chimney to the top of the icefall. Stay in the gully line on the right side of the wall; the rock step that follows is the only way onto the glacier tongue above.

A short band of easy fifth-class rock with no protection leads from the top of the icefall onto the narrow glacier tongue. Climb it with care, likely in crampons; with no gear, a slip here would run back down the icefall.
Steep snow on the tongue leads to a second large transverse crevasse. It crosses easily on its left end; do not try to force it in the middle.

The steepest sustained ground of the lower route: ice that starts around 60° and steepens to about 70° near the top, turning to snow before the base of the rock headwall. Pickets and screws both have a place here depending on how much snow covers the ice.

At the base of the headwall traverse left to a less-than-vertical weakness and climb it on fourth-class rock to a ledge. From the ledge traverse left around a corner to reach the foot of the long buttress.

A long buttress of easy fifth-class climbing on good, solid rock with positive holds, climbed for roughly its whole height to the crest of the main SE Ridge south of the Hourglass. A minimal rack of nuts and extra-long slings covers it.
Drop off the east side of the rocky SE Ridge crest onto the Sulphide Glacier and follow it north to the south side of the summit pyramid. Rope up for the glacier; it is crevassed.

Climb the summit pyramid by the regular fourth-class line, or take a direct line of roughly 800 ft of easy fifth-class rock. In low visibility on the way down, stay high and traverse directly below the Hourglass to avoid the Upper Curtis icefall.
